C005.subject: Intermittent fasting with a structured behavioral support program
C005.object: long-term weight loss compared to intermittent fasting alone
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting with a structured behavioral support program long-term weight loss compared to intermittent fasting alone]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting with behavioral support (e.g., group coaching, mobile app reminders) versus intermittent fasting alone in overweight adults over 12 months, with adherence and weight loss as primary endpoints. — Direct empirical test of the hypothesis: a well-designed RCT can isolate the effect of added behavioral support on adherence and subsequent long-term weight loss, providing causal evidence.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing behavioral interventions combined with dietary regimens for weight loss, focusing on adherence metrics and long-term outcomes. — Synthesizing published evidence from similar interventions (e.g., behavioral support for calorie restriction) can reveal whether adherence-mediated weight loss effects generalize to intermittent fasting, and identify effect size heterogeneity.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of health behavior change (e.g., Self-Determination Theory or Social Cognitive Theory) applied to intermittent fasting adherence, predicting that structured support enhances autonomous motivation and habit formation. — A theoretical framework can specify mechanisms (e.g., self-efficacy, social support) by which behavioral support improves adherence, offering testable predictions and guiding future empirical designs.

scope.domain: overweight and obese adults in community settings

C006.subject: Intermittent fasting
C006.object: daily caloric restriction for long-term weight loss, even in individuals with high adherence
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting daily caloric restriction for long-term weight loss, even in individuals with high adherence]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2 or time-restricted eating) vs. continuous caloric restriction over ≥12 months with objectively measured adherence (e.g., via continuous glucose monitors or urinary biomarkers) in overweight/obese adults — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing long-term weight loss outcomes between the two interventions in a high-adherence population, reducing confounding from self-reported compliance.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of long-term (≥1 year) studies on intermittent fasting vs. daily caloric restriction, stratified by adherence level (e.g., using subgroup analysis or meta-regression) — Aggregates existing evidence to assess whether the effect holds across diverse populations and adherence measures, addressing the disputed status with higher statistical power.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of energy balance and metabolic adaptation under intermittent vs. continuous restriction, incorporating adherence-dependent compliance curves — Provides mechanistic predictions for why intermittent fasting might or might not differ from daily restriction when adherence is high, helping to interpret empirical findings and guide future study design.

C007.subject: Intermittent fasting with a structured behavioral maintenance program
C007.object: weight regain at 12 months compared to continuous calorie restriction without such support
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting with a structured behavioral maintenance program weight regain at 12 months compared to continuous calorie restriction without such support]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting with behavioral maintenance program vs. continuous calorie restriction with standard follow-up in overweight adults with high baseline dietary adherence, measuring weight change at 12 months. — Directly tests the hypothesis under controlled conditions, addressing the specific comparison and population scope.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral maintenance interventions (e.g., self-monitoring, relapse prevention) combined with dietary regimens, focusing on long-term weight outcomes. — Synthesizes existing evidence on the additive effect of structured maintenance programs on weight regain, providing broader support or refutation across studies.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study examining adherence patterns and weight trajectories in overweight adults practicing intermittent fasting vs. continuous calorie restriction with or without behavioral support. — Provides real-world evidence on sustainability and weight regain, complementing RCT findings with ecological validity.

scope.domain: overweight adults with high baseline dietary adherence

C008.subject: Intermittent fasting
C008.object: lower weight regain than continuous calorie restriction after 12 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting lower weight regain than continuous calorie restriction after 12 months]

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of randomized controlled trials comparing intermittent fasting vs. continuous calorie restriction with ≥12-month follow-up weight data — A comprehensive meta-analysis of existing RCTs with long-term follow-up can directly compare weight regain rates between the two dietary approaches, addressing the disputed claim with aggregated empirical evidence.

[PATH:empirical] Prospective cohort study tracking weight trajectories over 12 months post-intervention in free-living individuals who completed structured intermittent fasting or continuous calorie restriction programs — This would provide real-world evidence in the specified general population without structured support, capturing adherence, metabolic adaptation, and behavioral factors that influence weight regain.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of appetite-regulating hormone dynamics (e.g., ghrelin, leptin, GLP-1) comparing intermittent vs. continuous energy restriction patterns — Understanding the physiological mechanisms—such as differential effects on satiety hormones or metabolic flexibility—could explain or predict differences in weight regain, helping to confirm or refute the hypothesis at a mechanistic level.

C011.subject: Intermittent fasting combined with high-protein intake
C011.object: metabolic adaptation that reduces long-term weight loss efficacy
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting combined with high-protein intake metabolic adaptation that reduces long-term weight loss efficacy]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., 16:8) with vs. without high-protein supplementation, measuring changes in resting metabolic rate and lean body mass over 12 months via DXA and indirect calorimetry. — Directly tests whether high-protein intake attenuates the metabolic adaptation (decline in RMR and lean mass) typically observed in prolonged intermittent fasting, providing causal evidence for or against the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing RCTs on intermittent fasting combined with protein intake, focusing on outcomes of metabolic adaptation (e.g., RMR, energy expenditure, fat-free mass preservation) in overweight/obese adults. — Synthesizes available evidence across multiple studies to assess consistency and effect size, addressing the disputed status with higher statistical power and generalizability.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic study using stable isotope tracers (e.g., 13C-leucine) to quantify whole-body protein turnover and mitochondrial efficiency during intermittent fasting with high-protein intake versus standard protein intake. — Elucidates the underlying physiological mechanisms (e.g., enhanced protein synthesis, reduced muscle catabolism, thermic effect of protein) that could explain if and how high-protein intake counteracts metabolic adaptation, informing plausibility of the hypothesis.

qualifier.rationale: High-protein intake may preserve lean mass and resting metabolic rate, counteracting the adaptation seen in standard intermittent fasting protocols.

C012.subject: Intermittent fasting
C012.object: metabolic adaptation that reduces long-term weight loss efficacy
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Intermittent fasting metabolic adaptation that reduces long-term weight loss efficacy]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., alternate-day fasting or time-restricted eating) versus continuous caloric restriction over 12+ months, measuring resting metabolic rate and weight loss trajectory at multiple time points. — Directly tests whether intermittent fasting attenuates the decline in metabolic rate typically seen with prolonged caloric restriction, which would confirm or refute the hypothesis about preventing metabolic adaptation.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies on intermittent fasting and energy expenditure, focusing on changes in resting metabolic rate, adaptive thermogenesis, and fat-free mass preservation. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether intermittent fasting consistently shows a protective effect against metabolic adaptation across different populations and protocols, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic study in animal models or human tissue examining the impact of intermittent fasting on pathways known to regulate metabolic adaptation, such as leptin signaling, thyroid hormone axis, or mitochondrial efficiency. — Provides biological plausibility and causal evidence for the proposed effect, helping to clarify whether any observed prevention is due to fasting-specific mechanisms rather than general caloric restriction.

qualifier.temporal: short-term (up to 12 weeks) and in early phases of weight loss intervention
